senses.gloss:
Śacīvant is apparently the name of a man in one passage of
the Rigveda,^1 where the vocative Śacīvaḥ occurs. But Roth^2
prefers to read Śacī ca instead.
1) x. 74. 5.
2) St. Petersburg Dictionary, s.v.
Cf. Ludwig, Translation of the Rig-
veda, 3, 108; Griffith, Hymns of the
Rigveda, 2, 489, n.

Saciva ‘companion,’ ‘attendant’ (from sac, ‘follow’), later a
common word for the comrade of a king, his minister, is found
in Vedic literature in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (iii. 20, 1), where
it is used by Indra of the Maruts. It seems to correspond in
sense to the German comes or the English gesith.^1
1) Stubbs, Select Charters, 57.

Sācī-guṇa is mentioned, apparently as a place in the territory
of the Bharatas, in a verse occurring in the Aitareya Brāh-
maṇa.^1 Leumann,^2 however, thinks an epithet of Indra,
Śācīgu, may be meant.
1) viii. 23, 4.
2) Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgen-
ländischen Gesellschaft, 48, 80, n. 5. This
conjecture seems improbable.
